intro: This last unit turns the course around. For sixteen units you have read the Tanakh as a book: its three parts, its stories, its laws, its poems and its commentators. Now you will watch it leave the page. A tiny scroll on a doorpost, a prayer book made of verses, a Passover table built on four lines of Deuteronomy, a spiritual sung in a field, a verse cast on the Liberty Bell, a rabbi speaking in Chicago in 1893. The first chapter follows the text into prayer, the calendar, the home and the wider world. It always describes how Jewish tradition and others have used it.

The second chapter is your capstone. You will choose a short passage and read it in two translations. You will map its structure and its silences. Then you will bring the commentators to the table: Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban, a midrash and a modern reader. From that you will build a thesis about what the text does and how it has been read. You will cite every claim by book, chapter and verse, and state other readings fairly. Then you will present it in chavruta, the traditional way of learning by arguing in pairs.

By the end you will be able to explain how the Tanakh lives in Jewish practice and in American speech. You will also have done, once, in your own voice, what its readers have done for two thousand years. You will have read a verse closely and heard the people who read it before you. And you will have said something about it that another careful reader can check.
bigQuestion: How does a text keep living in the practices, arguments and speech of the people who read it, and how do you join that conversation honestly?

timeline.t: The Mishnah is edited; its first tractate opens with rules for reciting the Shema
Genesis Rabbah gathers midrash on Genesis, filling the text's gaps with stories
Amram Gaon's order of prayers, the earliest surviving complete siddur
Rashi dies in Troyes; his commentary becomes the one Jewish readers open first
Ramban dies; his commentary answers Rashi and Ibn Ezra on the same page
The Tsene-rene retells the Torah portions in Yiddish for everyday readers
Chicago's first Jewish congregation, Kehilath Anshe Ma'arav, is founded
Enslaved singers' spiritual "Go Down, Moses" is first published
The World's Parliament of Religions meets in Chicago
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its English Tanakh, this course's text
Abington v. Schempp allows objective study of the Bible in public schools; King quotes Amos in Washington
Robert Alter's The Art of Biblical Narrative brings literary reading to a wide audience

words.d: the Jewish prayer book, built largely of Tanakh verses and psalms set among rabbinic blessings
three Torah passages recited morning and evening, beginning with Deuteronomy 6:4, "Hear, O Israel"
one of the 54 weekly Torah portions in the yearly reading cycle
the Passover telling, which expounds Deuteronomy 26:5-8 phrase by phrase
five short scrolls of the Ketuvim, each read on a holiday: Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther
the parchment with Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and 11:13-21 fixed in a case to a doorpost
the plain sense of a text, read in its order and context
interpretive reading that fills gaps and draws lessons, often through midrash
something a narrative leaves unsaid, which readers fill or leave open
a leading word that repeats through a passage to carry meaning; Buber and Rosenzweig's term
naming whose reading or belief a statement is, so a paper describes readers instead of asserting claims
a study partner, and the method of learning a text by reading and arguing in pairs

test.q: Which three passages make up the Shema?
test.why: The Shema is two Deuteronomy passages and one from Numbers. Psalms 113-118 are Hallel.

test.q: What is Hallel, and when is it sung?
choices: Psalms 113-118, on festivals such as Passover
test.why: Hallel is Psalms 113-118, sung on festivals; the Mishnah already describes it at the Passover meal.

test.q: How many weekly Torah portions are in the yearly cycle, and where does it restart?
test.why: The Torah is divided into 54 parashot; Simchat Torah ends Deuteronomy and begins Genesis again.

test.q: Which passage does the Haggadah expound line by line, following Mishnah Pesachim 10:4?
test.why: The Mishnah directs the telling to expound "A wandering Aramean was my father" through the end of the passage.

test.q: Which Megillah is read on Tisha B'Av?
test.why: Lamentations, the poems over ruined Jerusalem, is chanted on the fast mourning the Temples.

test.q: What do tefillin hold that a mezuzah does not?
test.why: Tefillin hold four passages: the two Shema paragraphs shared with the mezuzah plus two from Exodus 13.

test.q: What does the anthem "Hatikvah" do with Ezekiel 37:11?
choices: It reverses "our hope is lost" into "our hope is not yet lost"
It quotes it word for word
It sets it to the tune of a psalm
test.why: The anthem answers the dry bones' despair with its opposite; knowing the verse changes how the line sounds.

test.q: Which verse is inscribed on the Liberty Bell, and in which translation?
test.why: The bell, cast in 1752, carries Leviticus 25:10 in King James wording, "Proclaim liberty throughout all the land."

test.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Abington v. Schempp (1963)?
choices: Public schools must teach the Tanakh
The Bible may not be mentioned in public schools
Devotional exercises are barred, but objective study of the Bible in a secular program is allowed
Only the KJV may be studied
test.why: Schempp is the legal frame for this course: study, not devotion.

test.q: A student's thesis reads: "Genesis 22 proves that faith is rewarded." What is the problem?
choices: It asserts a truth claim instead of describing what the text does and how readers read it
test.why: Capstone theses use verbs about the text, such as delays or withholds, not verbs about truth.

test.q: What is the difference between peshat and derash?
choices: Peshat is the plain sense in context; derash is interpretive filling, often through midrash
Peshat is Hebrew; derash is Aramaic
Peshat is Rashi's method; derash is Ibn Ezra's
Peshat is prayer; derash is study
test.why: Rashi moves between both; Ibn Ezra and Rashbam lean toward peshat.

test.q: How does Genesis Rabbah fill the gap in Genesis 4:8, where Cain's words are missing?
choices: By adding "Let us go into the field" from the Greek
By supplying a quarrel over dividing the world
test.why: The midrash supplies a story; the Septuagint and Samaritan text supply a missing phrase instead.

test.q: Which commentator wrote a commentary that constantly answers Rashi and Ibn Ezra and hints at kabbalah?
test.why: Ramban (1194-1270) of Girona argues with both and marks mystical hints as secret.

test.q: How is a commentator cited in the capstone?
choices: By the page number of the printed book
By the year of his death
By the verse he comments on, such as "Ibn Ezra on Genesis 22:4"
test.why: Commentators are cited on the verse; Talmud by tractate and page; modern books by author, title and year.

test.q: What does chavruta train a student to do?
choices: State a partner's reading back fairly and sharpen a thesis through argument
test.why: Chavruta is paired study by argument; Ta'anit 7a reads "iron sharpeneth iron" as this sharpening.

write.prompt: Choose one verse this unit read closely (Genesis 22:2, Deuteronomy 26:5, Genesis 4:8 or Deuteronomy 6:8-9). Quote it in JPS 1917. What does the text do with its words, and how have two readers read it? Cite the verse, one commentator on it (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban or a midrash by collection and section) and one practice or modern reader from the unit, and state one reading that differs from yours.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse every time you quote or refer to the text, and the translation and year when you quote.
Attribute every reading: "Rashi reads," "the Haggadah takes," "Trible asks," never "the verse means" without a reader.
Use verbs about the text, such as delays, repeats, withholds, and avoid verbs about truth, such as proves or reveals.
State the strongest other reading before you answer it, and say what it sees that yours does not.
Keep the unit's terms exact: peshat, derash, gap, Leitwort, Megillot, chavruta.
